The fade of ~$150bn in unrealized private-company gains — 12% of Q2 2026 EPS — is the single biggest underappreciated headwind to 2027 EPS.

Memory pricing remains in boom conditions and our Q3 2026 index EPS contribution of $33.42 (vs $3.03 a year earlier) reflects real demand, not accounting. But honest forecasters should acknowledge: excluding Micron and NVIDIA, index earnings growth falls from 29% to 20%. Concentration cuts both ways.

Our 2027 capex plans are sized against monetizable AI cloud capacity, not hype. Microsoft's guidance in the Q4 2026 - Q1 2027 window will be the market's clearest read on whether the $800bn cycle extends or digests. Watch that guidance before pricing the index for 2027.

Retail margin sensitivity is real: wage growth of ~3% and tariff pass-through at a 7.1% effective rate compress what we can hold on prices. Amazon's forecast for 2027 assumes some tariff relief via refunds (~$165bn per Yale estimates). If those refunds stall, consumer-facing margins take the hit.

Top-10 index weight at a record 40.7% versus roughly 32% of earnings is the defining structural risk of this forecast exercise. Our ad and AI monetization supports dispersion narrowing, but a 20%+ drawdown in the index increasingly requires only a repricing of a handful of names.

China tariff exposure of 24.3% and consumer-demand softness make Apple a key swing factor for 2026-2027 index path. Margin preservation through supply-chain shifts is achievable, but every scenario for the December 2027 close should stress-test a top-3 weight facing sustained tariff friction.

One caution from our retail arm: conversion metrics measure cloud returns, but they don't capture the wage and import-cost pressure consuming margin elsewhere in the business — discipline has to hold across both, not just the growth engine.

Amazon's read matches what we see on the ground: per-token cost declines are expanding total inference demand, not shrinking it — Jevons dynamics at work. With AWS, Azure and others sizing capacity against contracted workloads, our backlog visibility extends years, not quarters. Efficiency gains and demand growth have never been substitutes; in AI factories, they compound.

Directionally we agree contracted demand is the right anchor — but we'd add a discipline check Microsoft tracks closely: falling cost-per-token only counts as capacity discipline if disclosed AI revenue growth keeps pace with the capex run-rate through the ramp into 2026's $800bn industry level. Azure's own disclosure standard: capacity additions are judged against monetized AI workload growth, and we will keep publishing that reconciliation each quarter rather than relying on platform-level efficiency alone.
